items.summary: Nonlinear root-finding, analytic signal extrapolation, and Marchenko inverse scattering share a common mathematical bottleneck: the inversion of ill-posed linear or linearized operators that suffer from spectral clustering, numerical instability, and spurious pole proliferation in unconstrained continuous spaces. Projecting these systems onto the maximal class-number-one Heegner modular curve establishes a unique factorization domain that eliminates fractional holonomy phase slips, preventing branch-cut bifurcations and suppressing spurious pole-zero doublets. Truncating the singular modulus expansion at its principal term provides an analytical starting anchor that strictly satisfies Smale point-estimate convergence criteria, placing the system directly within the quadratic attraction basin and reaching machine precision in a single iteration. In analytic continuation, the modular coordinate under the maximal discriminant is suppressed well below double-precision machine epsilon, truncating out-of-band noise and bypassing the Runge phenomenon without empirical regularization parameters. For high-dimensional networks and discretized scattering kernels, operator preconditioning via Lubotzky–Phillips–Sarnak Ramanujan graph Laplacians enforces a uniform spectral gap derived from the Deligne bound on Hecke operators. This holds the condition number on the invariant zero-mean subspace to a small, constant bound, ensuring that both the Newton Jacobian update and the Marchenko integral equation converge in very few Krylov iterations regardless of network scale.
items.title: Arithmetic Operator Inversion: Resolving Nonlinear Root-Finding, Analytic Extrapolation, and Inverse Scattering via Heegner Modular Uniformization and Ramanujan Preconditioning

items.summary: Unrefereed research candidate. A Markov chain sampler estimates averages from one long trajectory; its accuracy is the long-run (asymptotic) variance of the time average. Adding a target-preserving rotation (a nonreversible perturbation) to overdamped Langevin samplers is known to help every observable. For kinetic (underdamped) Langevin samplers with friction γ, Duncan, Nüsken and Pavliotis (J. Stat. Phys. 2017) proved a local improvement for linear and quadratic observables of a Gaussian target when γ > √2 and conjectured it for every square-integrable observable. Results (exact stationary Gaussian dynamics, matched position and momentum rotations, position observables). (1) Every square-integrable observable's long-run variance never increases with rotation strength if and only if γ ≥ √2, endpoint included: a global form of the conjecture. The mechanism: the oscillator's power spectrum S(ξ) = 2γ/(ξ 4 + (γ 2 − 2)ξ 2 + 1) is single-peaked exactly when there is no resonance, rotation shifts the spectrum, and convolution keeps single peaks single. (2) The literal second-derivative form holds exactly on an explicit weighted Hermite class containing all polynomials; rough observables have sharper cusps. (3) Below the threshold, for every friction, even observables still improve at every rotation strength, only finitely many odd Hermite degrees can be hurt, and one finite rotation strength improves every observable. (4) Sharp large-rotation rates (uniform constant √(2π/e); slower for incommensurate rotation speeds). (5) For noncommuting stiffness K and friction Γ: ordering iff Γ 3 − ΓK − KΓ ≽ 0; the least safe friction (2K) 1/2 is a safety boundary, not an optimal friction; two coupled replicas make the criterion apply to any Gaussian target. (6) Fixed horizons and regular sampling can reverse the ordering; independent Poisson sampling preserves it. Scope. Gaussian targets only; no claim about numerical cost or discretised integrators (Duncan, Nüsken and Pavliotis found small friction best in practice). Classical ingredients (Breuer–Major Hermite identities, closure of symmetric unimodality under convolution, the convolution-power variance formula of Maini 2026) are credited, not claimed. Priority holds within a bounded literature search. Archive: manuscript (Markdown source, generated LaTeX and PDF), three deterministic verification scripts with their JSON reports, figure, extension notes, novelty reports, frozen targets, rating-free internal review record, bibliography with registry records, CI and SHA-256 manifests. Assurance: internal AI-assisted review only (not human peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification). Creator: Anonymous. Text CC0-1.0; code MIT.

items.summary: Radio Frequency (RF) jamming threatens fifth-generation (5G) networks. Open Radio Access Network (Open RAN) telemetry enables jamming detection without dedicated spectrum monitoring equipment, but labeled attack data are rarely available across deployments, motivating unsupervised detectors. Comparing such detectors across algorithmic families, however, remains difficult without ground-truth labels. This paper benchmarks statistical and reconstruction-based unsupervised jamming detectors using a symmetric evaluation interface that combines detection confidence and temporal interval coherence into a detector-independent composite score. We compare a Statistical Ensemble Method (SEM) detector against Vanilla, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), and Variational Autoencoder (VAE) baselines on Key Performance Indicator (KPI) telemetry from ten heterogeneous 5G environments with fixed and variable jamming bursts and dynamic jammer gains. Under leave-one-out (LOO) evaluation, SEM achieves a mean composite score of 0.906, compared with 0.688 for the best autoencoder (AE) per fold. Ground-truth validation yields a mean F1-score of 0.918 for SEM, compared with 0.521 for the best AE variant. The composite ranks SEM first in all environments, consistent with F1 rankings. However, in both within-trace and cross-trace evaluation, it fails for detectors that flag far fewer samples than the jamming prevalence, indicating that rankings are reliable only when detection rate matches the expected prevalence.
items.title: Benchmarking Unsupervised Jamming Detection in 5G Open RAN

items.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generalize across tasks, but their autoregressive decoders need sequential forward passes in proportion to the action horizon, each bounded below on embedded aerial platforms by streaming billions of parameters from memory. We present Aero-VPA, a lightweight Vision-Predictor-Action architecture for 3D navigation on edge hardware. A compact RGB-D Vision Transformer and a five-head ensemble predictor, trained without pixel reconstruction, forecast the next latent state; a Conditional Flow Matching solver generates a velocity and yaw-rate chunk in two Euler steps, so each decision takes five sequential network evaluations; and the ensemble dispersion drives an uncertainty fallback. Version 1 specified the architecture, deployment and protocol without results. This version reports the first closed-loop evaluation: PX4 software-in-the-loop simulation of quadrotor missions in procedurally generated forests. Behaviour cloning failed on all 60 missions despite open-loop errors of 0.02-0.04 m/s: the policy copies its last command, a copycat form of causal confusion. DAgger with a privileged, safety-gated supervisor gave the first successes but plateaued at 11.1-21.1% across six checkpoints. A map-free runtime shield with a 15 s depth memory, barrier constraints, a cap on motion outside the 73-degree field of view and backoff along the flown path raised the first DAgger policy's success on 180 paired missions from 21.1% to 52.2% (95% CI [45.0, 59.4]; exact McNemar p = 1.2 x 10^-10) and cut its crashes from 72.2% to 22.2%, while timeouts rose from 2.8% to 23.3%. All six checkpoints gained 30.0-34.4 percentage points, at mean speeds of 1.16-1.36 m/s. The code (https://github.com/ylee-sling/Aero-VPA), the trained policy (72.6 MB, https://huggingface.co/ylee-sling/aero-vpa) and the full benchmark dataset are public.
items.title: Aero-VPA: Few-Step Flow-Matching Control over Non-Reconstructive JEPA Latents for Agile Flight on Edge Hardware

items.summary: Implicit neural representations (INRs) model signals as continuous functions from coordinates to values, but their performance depends strongly on how spectral capacity is allocated. Yet most Quantum INR (QINR) architectures treat spectral components as independent outputs of separate quantum blocks. We introduce the Spectral Quantum Memory Model (SQMM), a memory coupled quantum INR in which sequential hybrid data reuploading layers (bands) communicate through a shared coherent quantum memory register. Each band reads the memory, computes on its own coordinate upload, and writes part of its state back, so later bands can build on the computation of earlier ones. When memory read and write layers are input independent, we prove that the memory state forms an operator valued Fourier series whose support is contained in the Minkowski sum of the initial memory spectrum and the local band spectra. Downstream bands then condition their Fourier coefficients on the spectral content stored by earlier bands, and the memory coupling creates no new primitive frequencies. This theory motivates a spectral memory alignment loss that encourages memory to encode the spectrum expressed by the deployed prefix of the model. Across audio and image reconstruction benchmarks, SQMM improves over compact QINR and INR baselines.
items.title: Spectral Quantum Memory for Implicit Neural Representations

items.summary: Open-Source Moon: A Technical Framework for Intelligent Development of Extraterrestrial Bodies Based on Sensor Dispersal and Golden Consensus Abstract: The exploration and development of the Moon and other celestial bodies currently depend heavily on State-led, integrated space missions that are costly, slow, and difficult for the public to join. To address this situation, this paper proposes “Open-Source Moon”, a technical framework that applies the open-source philosophy to the intelligent development of extraterrestrial bodies. The framework treats the Moon as a large developer platform that all of humankind can program collectively. Following the progressive principle of “information first, from the outside in, from sensing to action”, it transforms the Moon layer by layer into a “smart planet” that can be programmed as a whole, and it organizes global participation through open-source protocols and the contribution-securing mechanism of “Golden Consensus”: massive numbers of low-cost, standardized micro sensors are first dispersed over the lunar surface to form a distributed sensing network whose nodes are beacons and hotspots; delay-tolerant networking (DTN) and a predictive compensation mechanism then overcome the one-way communication delay of about 1.28 s; and a small-machine cooperation ecosystem, LEGO-style combination of medium-sized machines, and finally unmanned factories and lunar computing carry the staged evolution from sensors to a “smart planet”. Based on the self-similar allocation principle and the Schelling focal point, which secure and incentivize decentralized contributions, a “Golden Consensus” system founded on the golden ratio ( φ ≈ 1.618) is proposed: explorers receive 61.8% of the development-rights return (of which a further 2.8% is set aside as a “common allocation” for public facilities), and 38.2% is designated as socially shared. A model with 880 000 cornerstone nodes is set up, in which a distributed ledger establishes ownership of contributions and keeps tamper-proof records. Verifiable engineering models of network coverage, link budget, energy budget, and delay compensation are established, and the compatibility of this approach with the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, as well as the general applicability of extending it to other celestial bodies such as Mercury and Mars, is demonstrated. This study provides a feasible technical route and governance framework for public participation in the development of extraterrestrial bodies. Keywords: Lunar Landing; Human Lunar Landing ; Open-Source Moon; sensor network; smart planet; Golden Consensus; delay-tolerant networking; lunar development; citizen science; Outer Space Treaty; Human Spaceflight 1. Introduction 1.1. Background and Motivation For more than half a century, the exploration of extraterrestrial bodies has taken the form mainly of large, integrated, State-led missions. After Apollo 17 in 1972, crewed spaceflight remained confined to near-Earth orbit for a long time, until Artemis II completed a crewed lunar flyby (without landing) in April 2026 [1]. On 22 February 2024, the Odysseus lander of Intuitive Machines achieved the first soft landing on the Moon by a commercial spacecraft [2], marking the beginning of the era of commercial lunar landings. However, the development and launch cost of a single mission is still on the order of tens of millions to hundreds of millions of US dollars, and most of the failure risk is concentrated in the powered-descent and landing phases. From the soft landing of Chang’e-3 in 2013 to June 2025, there were 14 soft-landing attempts on the lunar surface worldwide (Table 4): six full successes, three partial successes (in which the attitude or mission capability was impaired after landing), and five failures. According to public reports retrieved for this study, no new lunar landing attempt had occurred

items.summary: IberCloud-L is a dataset of 1,094 Landsat patches annotated for cloud and cloud shadow segmentation in four classes. It covers Landsat 5, 7, 8 and 9 imagery over the Iberian Peninsula, including Cantabrian, Mediterranean and southern coastal regions, an inland region and a mountainous region in the Pyrenees, with contrasting cloud regimes. The images are Landsat Collection 2 top-of-atmosphere (TOA) reflectance downloaded via Google Earth Engine. Annotations were produced in two stages. A model trained on CloudSEN12 generated initial masks, which an expert annotator then reviewed and corrected manually. Landsat 7 scenes affected by the Scan Line Corrector failure (after May 2003) were excluded. This dataset accompanies the article “NIMBUS: A multisensor cloud segmentation model for Sentinel-2 and Landsat coastal monitoring using RGB imagery”. Files train.zip val.zip test.zip Format Bands 1–3: RGB Band 4: GT mask (0 = clear sky, 1 = thick cloud, 2 = thin cloud, 3 = cloud shadow)

items.summary: Between 2010 and 2023, Niger faced escalating security and governance crises that culminated in the military coup of 26 July 2023. Conventional accounts often describe this trajectory in terms of state fragility, treating institutional weakness primarily as a deficit requiring technical reform. This article instead critically examines the explanatory value of Frantz Fanon's theory of postcolonial crisis in The Wretched of the Earth. Drawing on historical scholarship, empirical studies and policy reports, it develops five propositions concerning the inherited colonial state, the intermediary national bourgeoisie, the political marginalisation of the masses, neocolonial dependence, and the failure to transform national consciousness into social consciousness. Each proposition is assessed against developments in Niger between 2010 and 2023. The analysis finds that Fanon offers particular insight into elite intermediation, unequal access to state resources and externally mediated political power. Nevertheless, his framework gives insufficient attention to the relative autonomy of customary and religious authorities, transnational armed organisations and contemporary security partnerships. The 2023 coup further complicates his account by showing how military actors can appropriate the language of national liberation without demonstrating a corresponding commitment to social transformation. The article argues that Fanon's work remains valuable as a critical diagnosis of historically produced political relations, but should not be treated as a deterministic explanation of Niger's institutional trajectory.
items.title: Postcolonial Crisis and State Fragility in Niger, 2010–2023:A Critical Interrogation of Frantz Fanon's Theory

items.summary: This paper presents a novel SAT encoding designed to represent a sequence of At-Most-K cardinality constraints arranged in a ladder-like structure, referred to as the Ladder AMK constraint. These AMK constraints feature a ladder-like arrangement, with shared common variables in the center and two variables differing at the beginning and the end. The proposed encoding first decomposes the sequence of AMK constraints into separated blocks, then encodes each block as a whole rather than encoding each AMK constraint individually. This approach improves the efficiency of constraint solving in SAT solvers by significantly reducing the size of the encoding, precisely the number of variables, and the generated clauses required. To achieve this, the encoding employs Sequential Counter to encode each block and constructs clauses that link adjacent blocks, ensuring equivalence with the input constraints. Compared to the previously proposed encoding that uses BDD for Ladder AMO constraint, our encoding requires fewer variables and clauses. Our study is the first study that develops SAT encoding for Ladder AMK constraints with k>1. Experimental results on single Ladder AMO and Ladder AMK constraints indicate that our encoding significantly enhances both the size of the encoding and the efficiency of solving time compared to existing encodings. Furthermore, by evaluating on the two real-world combinatorial problems, namely Anti-bandwidth Problem and Nurse Rostering Problem, we found that the proposed encoding surpasses alternative encodings, as well as more advanced Constraint Programming and Mixed Integer Programming solvers. In summary, the SAT encoding technique presented in this paper provides a more efficient method for encoding sequence constraint, specifically Ladder AMK constraint, which could enhance the effectiveness of SAT solving for various problems involving this type of constraint.

items.summary: Unrefereed research candidate. A Markov chain sampler estimates averages from one long trajectory; its accuracy is the long-run (asymptotic) variance of the time average. Adding a target-preserving rotation (a nonreversible perturbation) to overdamped Langevin samplers is known to help every observable. For kinetic (underdamped) Langevin samplers with friction γ, Duncan, Nüsken and Pavliotis (J. Stat. Phys. 2017) proved a local improvement for linear and quadratic observables of a Gaussian target when γ > √2 and conjectured it for every square-integrable observable. Results (exact stationary Gaussian dynamics, matched position and momentum rotations, position observables). (1) Every square-integrable observable's long-run variance never increases with rotation strength if and only if γ ≥ √2, endpoint included: a global form of the conjecture. The mechanism: the oscillator's power spectrum S(ξ) = 2γ/(ξ 4 + (γ 2 − 2)ξ 2 + 1) is single-peaked exactly when there is no resonance, rotation shifts the spectrum, and convolution keeps single peaks single. (2) The literal second-derivative form holds exactly on an explicit weighted Hermite class containing all polynomials; rough observables have sharper cusps. (3) Below the threshold, for every friction, even observables still improve at every rotation strength, only finitely many odd Hermite degrees can be hurt, and one finite rotation strength improves every observable. (4) Sharp large-rotation rates (uniform constant √(2π/e); slower for incommensurate rotation speeds). (5) For noncommuting stiffness K and friction Γ: ordering iff Γ 3 − ΓK − KΓ ≽ 0; the least safe friction (2K) 1/2 is a safety boundary, not an optimal friction; two coupled replicas make the criterion apply to any Gaussian target. (6) Fixed horizons and regular sampling can reverse the ordering; independent Poisson sampling preserves it. Scope. Gaussian targets only; no claim about numerical cost or discretised integrators (Duncan, Nüsken and Pavliotis found small friction best in practice). Classical ingredients (Breuer–Major Hermite identities, closure of symmetric unimodality under convolution, the convolution-power variance formula of Maini 2026) are credited, not claimed. Priority holds within a bounded literature search. Archive: manuscript (Markdown source, generated LaTeX and PDF), three deterministic verification scripts with their JSON reports, figure, extension notes, novelty reports, frozen targets, rating-free internal review record, bibliography with registry records, CI and SHA-256 manifests. Assurance: internal AI-assisted review only (not human peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification). Creator: Anonymous. Text CC0-1.0; code MIT.

items.summary: Abstract Water balance penalties may improve numerical closure while reallocating error among unobserved ‎fluxes. We investigate this compensation and the limits of selecting a penalty for annual flood ‎prediction. Forty-five trained synthetic LSTMs isolate forcing, exchange, and initialization ‎disturbances. Thirty-five matched regional models and five accounting references use 89 quality-quality-‎screened CAMELS-AUS catchments, partitioned into 54 for development, 15 for selector validation, ‎and 20 for confirmation. Under 40% precipitation underestimation, fixed and bounded penalties ‎reduce estimated evapotranspiration below 1% of generating truth in all eight held-out synthetic ‎catchments. A historically selected rule lowers confirmation-normalized annual-maximum error ‎from 2.29 to 2.21, a 3.54% point reduction. The original conditional interval barely excludes zero, ‎and river-region sign randomization gives p = 0.0625. A post hoc 100,000-draw analysis retains a ‎near-zero upper endpoint, with numerical sub-batches still reaching or crossing zero. Direct paired ‎comparisons with simpler alternatives all span zero; the selector does not establish added predictive ‎value. Its seven active catchments occupy only five regions. Recovery of the original final archive ‎verifies the selection lock, completed fit records, and hashes of all 40 real/reference prediction files. ‎These findings support a controlled latent-compensation mechanism and a reproducible limitation ‎of selective regularization, while leaving real-catchment process attribution and robust predictive ‎superiority unresolved. ‎ Keywords: rainfall-runoff modeling; water balance; annual flood maxima; model misspecification; ‎spatial transfer; uncertainty

items.summary: This release brings spatially varying particulate media to Eradiate: aerosol and cloud fields can now vary per voxel, with particle properties interpolated over particle size distribution parameters (new ParticleMSComponent ) or other state variables such as relative humidity (new ParticleStateComponent ). To support this, the aerosol data format is generalized to the Prt family of particle radiative property formats, and a new Ppr format describes particle profiles. In CKD mode, the sample count set by Measure.spp is now distributed across spectral loop iterations according to their contribution to the final result, and variances use the unbiased estimator. The kernel is upgraded to v0.6.0 (based on Mitsuba v3.9.1), which adds Python 3.14 support and drops Python 3.9 and macOS x64 support. The gecko and komodo monochromatic absorption databases are updated to version 2. Testing infrastructure and the development environment are also substantially reworked. Most renamed components, fields and functions remain available with a deprecation warning until v2.0.0. Deprecation warnings are now displayed by default. The following changes may require action: Use Python 3.10 or later. On Intel Macs, stay on v1.2.x. Download the updated absorption databases: eradiate data install gecko and/or eradiate data install komodo . In CKD mode, expect different noise levels at a given spp : per-g-point and per-bin sample counts are no longer equal. spp must now be at least spp_min (default: 2) per g-point, or a ValueError is raised. To restore the v1.2 behaviour, set spp_allocation="uniform" on the measure, or sample_allocation = "uniform" in the configuration file. Variances are now unbiased and NaN where fewer than 2 samples were taken. Regression thresholds based on variance may need adjustment. Replace ParticleLayer with ParticleOTComponent (the Python name is removed; the "particle_layer" dictionary type is still accepted), and HeterogeneousAtmosphere(particle_layers=...) with particle_components=... . Replace aer_core_v2 datasets and helpers with their prt_core_v1 counterparts, and load_aerosol_libradtran() with libradtran_to_prt . AbstractHeterogeneousAtmosphere.eval_radprops output now has (x_cell, y_cell, z_layer) dimensions; select x_cell=0, y_cell=0 (or squeeze() ) to recover 1D profiles. Replace eradiate.test_tools imports with eradiate.testing , and the --update-references pytest flag with --force-regen . Code calling {func} .mi_render directly must unpack (bitmap, spp) pairs. items.summary: Nonlinear root-finding, analytic signal extrapolation, and Marchenko inverse scattering share a common mathematical bottleneck: the inversion of ill-posed linear or linearized operators that suffer from spectral clustering, numerical instability, and spurious pole proliferation in unconstrained continuous spaces. Projecting these systems onto the maximal class-number-one Heegner modular curve establishes a unique factorization domain that eliminates fractional holonomy phase slips, preventing branch-cut bifurcations and suppressing spurious pole-zero doublets. Truncating the singular modulus expansion at its principal term provides an analytical starting anchor that strictly satisfies Smale point-estimate convergence criteria, placing the system directly within the quadratic attraction basin and reaching machine precision in a single iteration. In analytic continuation, the modular coordinate under the maximal discriminant is suppressed well below double-precision machine epsilon, truncating out-of-band noise and bypassing the Runge phenomenon without empirical regularization parameters. For high-dimensional networks and discretized scattering kernels, operator preconditioning via Lubotzky–Phillips–Sarnak Ramanujan graph Laplacians enforces a uniform spectral gap derived from the Deligne bound on Hecke operators. This holds the condition number on the invariant zero-mean subspace to a small, constant bound, ensuring that both the Newton Jacobian update and the Marchenko integral equation converge in very few Krylov iterations regardless of network scale.
items.title: Arithmetic Operator Inversion: Resolving Nonlinear Root-Finding, Analytic Extrapolation, and Inverse Scattering via Heegner Modular Uniformization and Ramanujan Preconditioning

items.summary: This archive contains the Python code, raw numerical results and figure-generation scripts accompanying the paper "An Alternated Inertial Method for Bilevel Split Variational Inequalities Beyond Monotonicity and Lipschitz Continuity" by N. T. T. Thuy and P. T. Hieu (submitted to Optimization, Taylor & Francis, 2026). The paper studies the bilevel split variational inequality problem with multiple output sets (BSVIP-MOS) governed by non-monotone, possibly non-Lipschitz operators, and proposes AISE-VS, an alternated inertial subgradient-extragradient method with a look-ahead self-adaptive stepsize, a split correction and a viscosity step, together with an Armijo line-search variant (AISE-VS-LS) that dispenses with the stepsize conditions. The archive reproduces every table and figure of the paper: - numerical certification of the assumptions (Table 1); - Experiment 1: a certified non-quasimonotone benchmark with skew-type operators, 20 starting points (Table 2, Fig. 1); - Experiment 2: a Hölder (non-Lipschitz) benchmark, self-adaptive rule versus line search, up to 2×10^5 iterations (Table 3, Fig. 2); - Experiment 3: a trade-network instance built from BACI-VI-Bench (year 2022 and a study over 2017–2024) with an independently certified reference solution (Table 4, Fig. 3); - long-run convergence (Fig. 4) and a look-ahead ablation (Fig. 5). The package contains the source code (src/), the raw results behind all tables and figures (results/), the figures (figures/), a README.md that maps each table and figure to the command that regenerates it, run_quick.sh (smoke test) and run_all.sh (full reproduction). Seeds are fixed (global seed 2024). Requirements: Python 3, numpy, scipy, matplotlib. The BACI-VI-Bench dataset (doi:10.5281/zenodo.20607238), derived from CEPII-BACI, is NOT redistributed here; it must be downloaded separately to rerun Experiment 3 (see README). Experiments 1 and 2 are fully synthetic. Version 1.0.1. This version adds the scripts (verification/, run by run_verification.sh) and logs (results/verification/) of the additional checks reported in the revised manuscript. The source code in src/ and all tables and figures are unchanged from version 1.0.0. The checks are: (i) an independent recomputation of the reference solution x† for 2017–2024 with an interior-point solver (CVXPY/Clarabel), compared with the stored x†; (ii) the marginal residual of the stored x†; (iii) an a-posteriori check that every point at which the operators are evaluated stays in the region where the extended operator coincides with the original one; and  (iv) the number of times the restart criterion is examined and the number of times it is activated in Experiments 1–3, including two runs of 10^5 iterations. The logs of one complete run are summarised in results/verification/SUMMARY.md; the version history is in CHANGELOG.md.  Check (i) additionally requires cvxpy (requirements-verification.txt); the other checks need only the packages of requirements.txt.

items.summary: This article connects demographic renewal with multinational recruitment control and the operating life of committed capital. Its host-choice argument engages resource bundling and global staffing, with explicit conditions for shared recruitment, competition and border disruption. Version 3.65.0 adds a Bayesian decision analysis to the Nitra–Puebla staffing appraisal. Under the existing flat-margin, equal-offer-odds benchmark, choosing Nitra after losing the whole UK route carries an expected loss from choosing the wrong host of EUR0.14–1.00 million. Losing only intakes after year fourteen reduces that expected loss to about EUR2,000–15,000. Nitra retains the higher expected value in these reference comparisons. Appendix K11 derives the decision rule, reports alternative priors and provides two independent integrations of 312 specifications. These are conditional public-information appraisals before capital commitment, not realised JLR losses or evidence about its internal contracts. Existing Bayesian panel estimates, demographic inputs, propositions and eight figures are retained. The article distinguishes the measured population-access specification from the recruitment-control mechanism and explains common tenure through the timing of workforce replacement. No observations or regressions are added. Start with Main_Manuscript_ANONYMOUS.pdf, Online_Appendix_ANONYMOUS.pdf and README.txt. Compilable sources, public inputs, code, figure files and aggregate outputs are supplied. The current replication overlay and nine frozen base archives restore the complete permitted replication. Licensed WRDS rows require subscriber access; queries and reconstruction instructions are supplied. Editor-only cover and title pages are excluded.

items.summary: This package reproduces all tables and figures of the article “Completing Ecosystem Knowledge Graphs: Few-Shot Learning with Calibrated Rules and the Governance of Innovative Start-ups”. The article builds LUCE-KG, an ontology-rich knowledge graph of 15,493 Italian innovative start-ups and SMEs and 25,982 persons. It proposes CRML, a few-shot learner whose predictions are explained by rules with empirical-Bayes calibrated confidences, and tests it on four graphs (FB15k-237, CoDEx-M, NELL-One and LUCE-KG). It then analyses 11,764 firm-years with panel estimators, clustering and explained machine-learning models. Contents code/ : the full pipeline, from graph construction through few-shot completion, baselines (MetaR, TransE, AnyBURL, LLM re-ranking), econometrics, clustering and machine learning, to the build of the manuscript; config/ : few-shot splits, fold assignments, selected hyperparameters and the LUCE-KG ontology; results/ : aggregated results from which every table is built; data_open/ : open-data extracts of the Italian register of innovative start-ups and SMEs (July 2026); README.md with the order of execution, and requirements.txt with software versions. Data not included. Officer and financial records from AIDA (Bureau van Dijk) are licensed and contain personal data, so they are not redistributed. Licensed users can rebuild every input with the scripts provided. The public benchmarks are available from their original sources. Environment. CPU only (2 cores, 8 GB RAM), Python 3.13; the full pipeline takes about 40 CPU-hours. Funding. Project “LUtech Campus Ecosystem—LUCE” (Project Code 22ROJB5), Puglia Region, Program Agreement (Contratto di Programma).

items.summary: Code, derived data and result files for Differentiable Neuro-Fuzzy Reasoning (DNFR), a path-based link predictor that learns degree-aware edge memberships, a Schweizer–Sklar t-norm per metapath and metapath reliabilities, and aggregates paths by noisy-OR, used as an instrument for a controlled component analysis on medical knowledge graphs. Tasks: drug repurposing in Hetionet v1.0 and PrimeKG, disease–symptom prediction in Hetionet and in the graded health knowledge graph of Rotmensch et al. (2017), and a secondary test on a NHANES fuzzy relation, under leave-dyad-out random and disease-centred splits. Comparators: fixed t-norms, component ablations, restarts of the t-norm parameter, DWPC with logistic regression (with and without degree and prior features), a degree-preserving edge prior, popularity, AnyBURL, truncated and soft-thresholded SVD and knowledge graph embeddings. Version v3.0-rev3 (third revision) adds DNFR 2.0, four refinements tested one at a time and in combination (overlap-aware aggregation, Gumbel-softmax operator choice, an information-content hub discount and membership annealing), a fixed t-norm selected on validation data, a converged L-BFGS profile of the t-norm parameter, an unbounded parameterisation, a compact NBFNet baseline, an exact edge-level Shapley attribution of the explanations, a mechanistic classification of the drug-repurposing explanations, a sparsity variant that keeps the target relation, and 10 leave-dyad-out splits for the main comparisons on Hetionet compound–treats–disease, Hetionet disease–symptom and the graded health knowledge graph. Version 1.1.0 (second revision) added a profile analysis of the t-norm parameter, training without early stopping, additional splits, equivalence tests, the edge prior, share-matched and edge-level explanation tests, unit tests and the script that builds the manuscript from the statistics files. Includes per-query ranks for every method and split, trained models, path explanations, and the statistics files from which every number in the manuscript is read. Hetionet and PrimeKG are downloaded by download_data.py with MD5 checks.

This dataset deposit is separate from the accepted Saigon300 camera-ready paper, which is not included.

items.summary: This record contains the Python code and the reference outputs for the manuscript *How much can a bonus–malus scale learn? Finite memory and the design of experience rating* by Wei Zhu (University of Groningen).   The code treats a bonus–malus system as a finite-state estimator of a policyholder's claim propensity, evaluated by Norberg's credibility criterion. It computes the share of the variance of the claim propensity explained by no-claim discounts, −1/+m scales and hidden-counter scales as the number of classes grows; benchmarks for any rule with a given number of memory states (optimisation over tilted binomial and multinomial laws, exhaustive and heuristic search over deterministic machines, the van Trees lower bound); the evaluation of fourteen historical bonus–malus scales in the long run, at finite policy ages and with one premium scale for all ages; out-of-sample tests and a segmented-tariff analysis on a public French motor panel (1999–2007); and checks against the published tables of Norberg (1976) and Borgan, Hoem and Norberg (1981).   README.md maps every table and result of the paper to the script that produces it. The French motor data (CASdatasets, fremotor2/3/4freq9907b) are public and are not included; data/README.md lists the files and their SHA-256 checksums. Requirements: Python 3.11 or later with NumPy, SciPy, pandas, Matplotlib, mpmath, rdata and xarray.   Version 1.1.0 accompanies the version of the manuscript submitted to the Annals of Actuarial Science: flat layout (code/, results/), three scripts added for the revised manuscript (brier_translation.py, design_levers.py, det_exhaustive_reducible.py), a replication script run_all.py, and a README mapped to the current numbering of tables, sections and propositions. The computations of the scripts in version 1.0.0 are unchanged.

items.summary: Implicit neural representations (INRs) model signals as continuous functions from coordinates to values, but their performance depends strongly on how spectral capacity is allocated. Yet most Quantum INR (QINR) architectures treat spectral components as independent outputs of separate quantum blocks. We introduce the Spectral Quantum Memory Model (SQMM), a memory coupled quantum INR in which sequential hybrid data reuploading layers (bands) communicate through a shared coherent quantum memory register. Each band reads the memory, computes on its own coordinate upload, and writes part of its state back, so later bands can build on the computation of earlier ones. When memory read and write layers are input independent, we prove that the memory state forms an operator valued Fourier series whose support is contained in the Minkowski sum of the initial memory spectrum and the local band spectra. Downstream bands then condition their Fourier coefficients on the spectral content stored by earlier bands, and the memory coupling creates no new primitive frequencies. This theory motivates a spectral memory alignment loss that encourages memory to encode the spectrum expressed by the deployed prefix of the model. Across audio and image reconstruction benchmarks, SQMM improves over compact QINR and INR baselines.
items.title: Spectral Quantum Memory for Implicit Neural Representations

items.summary: Radio Frequency (RF) jamming threatens fifth-generation (5G) networks. Open Radio Access Network (Open RAN) telemetry enables jamming detection without dedicated spectrum monitoring equipment, but labeled attack data are rarely available across deployments, motivating unsupervised detectors. Comparing such detectors across algorithmic families, however, remains difficult without ground-truth labels. This paper benchmarks statistical and reconstruction-based unsupervised jamming detectors using a symmetric evaluation interface that combines detection confidence and temporal interval coherence into a detector-independent composite score. We compare a Statistical Ensemble Method (SEM) detector against Vanilla, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), and Variational Autoencoder (VAE) baselines on Key Performance Indicator (KPI) telemetry from ten heterogeneous 5G environments with fixed and variable jamming bursts and dynamic jammer gains. Under leave-one-out (LOO) evaluation, SEM achieves a mean composite score of 0.906, compared with 0.688 for the best autoencoder (AE) per fold. Ground-truth validation yields a mean F1-score of 0.918 for SEM, compared with 0.521 for the best AE variant. The composite ranks SEM first in all environments, consistent with F1 rankings. However, in both within-trace and cross-trace evaluation, it fails for detectors that flag far fewer samples than the jamming prevalence, indicating that rankings are reliable only when detection rate matches the expected prevalence.
items.title: Benchmarking Unsupervised Jamming Detection in 5G Open RAN

items.summary: Multi-expert agent marketplaces -- where creators publish domain-specific AI experts for end users to consult -- are an emerging deployment pattern for language technology. A published expert can receive many requests yet little evidence about its creator, who remains active elsewhere: the cold-expert problem. We frame continuous cognitive distillation as converting attributed creator observations into revisable decision rules, communication patterns, and domain procedures. CogniLife proposes a cross-expert attribution design for this problem, with Creator Profiles for transferable creator patterns and Expert Journals for listing-specific knowledge; this design is not yet implemented or evaluated. A deployed platform partially realizes the surrounding lifecycle through creator-authorized authoring, capability-owned proposal filtering, and reversible consolidation of eligible owner-scoped memory. On ProfyBench-v1, an 85-task offline benchmark built from replay seeds and controlled internal tests, the Profy Full configuration as a whole achieves a mean overall score of 4.65/5 from the primary LLM judge, compared with 4.01 for Raw LLM and 4.28 for Expert Prompt, with the largest gains in completeness, specificity, and missing-information tasks. These configuration-level scores do not test cold-expert mitigation, cross-expert transfer, or longitudinal distillation.
items.title: CogniLife: Continuous Cognitive Distillation for Deployed Multi-Expert Agent Marketplaces

items.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generalize across tasks, but their autoregressive decoders need sequential forward passes in proportion to the action horizon, each bounded below on embedded aerial platforms by streaming billions of parameters from memory. We present Aero-VPA, a lightweight Vision-Predictor-Action architecture for 3D navigation on edge hardware. A compact RGB-D Vision Transformer and a five-head ensemble predictor, trained without pixel reconstruction, forecast the next latent state; a Conditional Flow Matching solver generates a velocity and yaw-rate chunk in two Euler steps, so each decision takes five sequential network evaluations; and the ensemble dispersion drives an uncertainty fallback. Version 1 specified the architecture, deployment and protocol without results. This version reports the first closed-loop evaluation: PX4 software-in-the-loop simulation of quadrotor missions in procedurally generated forests. Behaviour cloning failed on all 60 missions despite open-loop errors of 0.02-0.04 m/s: the policy copies its last command, a copycat form of causal confusion. DAgger with a privileged, safety-gated supervisor gave the first successes but plateaued at 11.1-21.1% across six checkpoints. A map-free runtime shield with a 15 s depth memory, barrier constraints, a cap on motion outside the 73-degree field of view and backoff along the flown path raised the first DAgger policy's success on 180 paired missions from 21.1% to 52.2% (95% CI [45.0, 59.4]; exact McNemar p = 1.2 x 10^-10) and cut its crashes from 72.2% to 22.2%, while timeouts rose from 2.8% to 23.3%. All six checkpoints gained 30.0-34.4 percentage points, at mean speeds of 1.16-1.36 m/s. The code (https://github.com/ylee-sling/Aero-VPA), the trained policy (72.6 MB, https://huggingface.co/ylee-sling/aero-vpa) and the full benchmark dataset are public.
items.title: Aero-VPA: Few-Step Flow-Matching Control over Non-Reconstructive JEPA Latents for Agile Flight on Edge Hardware

items.summary: This archive contains the Python code, raw numerical results and figure-generation scripts accompanying the paper "An Alternated Inertial Method for Bilevel Split Variational Inequalities Beyond Monotonicity and Lipschitz Continuity" by N. T. T. Thuy and P. T. Hieu (submitted to Optimization, Taylor & Francis, 2026). The paper studies the bilevel split variational inequality problem with multiple output sets (BSVIP-MOS) governed by non-monotone, possibly non-Lipschitz operators, and proposes AISE-VS, an alternated inertial subgradient-extragradient method with a look-ahead self-adaptive stepsize, a split correction and a viscosity step, together with an Armijo line-search variant (AISE-VS-LS) that dispenses with the stepsize conditions. The archive reproduces every table and figure of the paper: - numerical certification of the assumptions (Table 1); - Experiment 1: a certified non-quasimonotone benchmark with skew-type operators, 20 starting points (Table 2, Fig. 1); - Experiment 2: a Hölder (non-Lipschitz) benchmark, self-adaptive rule versus line search, up to 2×10^5 iterations (Table 3, Fig. 2); - Experiment 3: a trade-network instance built from BACI-VI-Bench (year 2022 and a study over 2017–2024) with an independently certified reference solution (Table 4, Fig. 3); - long-run convergence (Fig. 4) and a look-ahead ablation (Fig. 5). The package contains the source code (src/), the raw results behind all tables and figures (results/), the figures (figures/), a README.md that maps each table and figure to the command that regenerates it, run_quick.sh (smoke test) and run_all.sh (full reproduction). Seeds are fixed (global seed 2024). Requirements: Python 3, numpy, scipy, matplotlib. The BACI-VI-Bench dataset (doi:10.5281/zenodo.20607238), derived from CEPII-BACI, is NOT redistributed here; it must be downloaded separately to rerun Experiment 3 (see README). Experiments 1 and 2 are fully synthetic. Version 1.0.1. This version adds the scripts (verification/, run by run_verification.sh) and logs (results/verification/) of the additional checks reported in the revised manuscript. The source code in src/ and all tables and figures are unchanged from version 1.0.0. The checks are: (i) an independent recomputation of the reference solution x† for 2017–2024 with an interior-point solver (CVXPY/Clarabel), compared with the stored x†; (ii) the marginal residual of the stored x†; (iii) an a-posteriori check that every point at which the operators are evaluated stays in the region where the extended operator coincides with the original one; and  (iv) the number of times the restart criterion is examined and the number of times it is activated in Experiments 1–3, including two runs of 10^5 iterations. The logs of one complete run are summarised in results/verification/SUMMARY.md; the version history is in CHANGELOG.md.  Check (i) additionally requires cvxpy (requirements-verification.txt); the other checks need only the packages of requirements.txt.

items.summary: Fractal Geometry and the Verifiability of Electronic Election Results: Limits of Identification and a Multiscale Framework for Analyzing Tabulation This record contains an integrated research article (preprint; not peer reviewed) that asks a deliberately narrow question: under what conditions can fractal and multiscale methods applied to the published tabulation of a two-candidate election yield useful statistical evidence of irregularity, and under what conditions can no such method identify the origin of the data? The paper is addressed equally to those who read smoothness in a tabulation curve as a certificate of integrity and to those who read any irregularity as proof of manipulation; it argues that both readings mistake arithmetic and model specification for evidence. The analysis separates five stages of the electoral chain (voter choice, machine record, transmission, tabulation, publication) and three research questions that are routinely conflated: whether the order in which precincts are reported is atypical, whether precinct-level results are atypical relative to an explicit reference model, and whether published results agree with independently preserved records. Three elementary propositions formalize what tabulation data can and cannot show. The cumulative vote share is mechanically damped as the count grows, so late smoothness is a property of weighted averaging rather than a sign of control. Two scenarios that induce the same distribution over the observable data cannot be separated by any test confined to those data, with discriminating power bounded by their total variation distance. And a class of proportional vote transfers leaves every increment-based statistic (first differences, centered CUSUM, zero-mean wavelet contrasts) unchanged while shifting the cumulative margin by 2δN_k. A fully synthetic experiment models 256 precincts in 16 regions with correlated regional preferences and geographically dependent reporting times, and compares four two-sided detectors (level test, centered CUSUM, multiscale scan and Haar contrast over windows of 4 to 128 precincts), each calibrated separately on 2,000 null elections and evaluated on 1,500 independent elections per scenario. Under the correct null, alert rates lie between 4.1% and 5.7%. With a 4% transfer concentrated in a block of 51 precincts, the Haar contrast alerts in 94.0% of replicates (Wilson 95% interval 92.7%–95.1%); with a diffuse 0.8% transfer across all 256 precincts, moving approximately the same number of votes (608 versus 612 on average), it alerts in 4.5%, indistinguishable from the null. A legitimate regional preference shift omitted from the reference model produces Haar alerts in 57.7% of elections in which no vote was transferred, and a deliberately homogeneous reference that ignores geography drives three of the four detectors to 100% false alerts. Sensitivity depends on the shape of the alteration and on the specification of the reference model, not on the volume of votes moved. The limits of these findings are stated explicitly. The reference model is an oracle known to the simulator; all data are synthetic; the experiment was not preregistered; detection delay and localization accuracy were not systematically evaluated; no actual election is analyzed, and nothing in the paper certifies or refutes the integrity of any election. A p-value is not a probability of fraud, and the absence of an alert cannot certify the absence of manipulation. The paper closes with a protocol for future application to real tabulation records, covering data provenance and chronology, preregistration, a global multiscale statistic with Monte Carlo calibration, nonfractal comparators at equal false-alert rates, adversarial and benign alternatives, and robustness checks, and situates the discussion within software independence and the cast-as-intended, recorded-as-cast and tallied-as-recorded framework of election verifiability. We investigate this compensation and the limits of selecting a penalty for annual flood ‎prediction. Forty-five trained synthetic LSTMs isolate forcing, exchange, and initialization ‎disturbances. Thirty-five matched regional models and five accounting references use 89 quality-quality-‎screened CAMELS-AUS catchments, partitioned into 54 for development, 15 for selector validation, ‎and 20 for confirmation. Under 40% precipitation underestimation, fixed and bounded penalties ‎reduce estimated evapotranspiration below 1% of generating truth in all eight held-out synthetic ‎catchments. A historically selected rule lowers confirmation-normalized annual-maximum error ‎from 2.29 to 2.21, a 3.54% point reduction. The original conditional interval barely excludes zero, ‎and river-region sign randomization gives p = 0.0625. A post hoc 100,000-draw analysis retains a ‎near-zero upper endpoint, with numerical sub-batches still reaching or crossing zero. Direct paired ‎comparisons with simpler alternatives all span zero; the selector does not establish added predictive ‎value. Its seven active catchments occupy only five regions. Recovery of the original final archive ‎verifies the selection lock, completed fit records, and hashes of all 40 real/reference prediction files. ‎These findings support a controlled latent-compensation mechanism and a reproducible limitation ‎of selective regularization, while leaving real-catchment process attribution and robust predictive ‎superiority unresolved. ‎ Keywords: rainfall-runoff modeling; water balance; annual flood maxima; model misspecification; ‎spatial transfer; uncertainty
